arml-1997-individual-01.title: Express everything with a and n
arml-1997-individual-01.body:
From $b-n=a+n$ we get $b=a+2n$, and $\frac cn=a+n$ gives $c=n(a+n)$. Then
$$a+b+c=2a+2n+n(a+n)=2(a+n)+n(a+n)=(n+2)(a+n)=19\cdot97=1843.$$
Since $19$ and $97$ are prime, $n+2\in\{1,19,97,1843\}$. $n+2=1$ gives $n<0$; for $n+2=97$ or $1843$ we would get $a+n\le19$ with $n\ge95$, so $a<0$. Hence $n+2=19$, $n=17$, $a+17=97$ and $a=80$.

**Answer: 80**

arml-1997-individual-02.title: Area as a quadratic in the height
arml-1997-individual-02.body:
By the extended Law of Sines $AC=2\cdot12\sin30^\circ=12$. Let $h$ be the distance from $B$ to line $AC$; the circle centred at $B$ tangent to $AC$ has radius $h$. Within the triangle, the circle covers a sector of angle $30^\circ$ at $B$ (the sides $BA$, $BC$ are at least $h$ long), of area $\frac1{12}\pi h^2$. So
$$\text{Area}(R)=\frac12\cdot12\cdot h-\frac{\pi h^2}{12}=6h-\frac{\pi}{12}h^2.$$
This quadratic is maximal at $h=\frac{6}{\pi/6}=\frac{36}\pi\approx11.5$, which is attainable because $B$ moves on the arc where $h$ takes every value up to $12+6\sqrt3\approx22.4$. The maximum is $6\cdot\frac{36}{\pi}-\frac{\pi}{12}\cdot\frac{36^2}{\pi^2}=\frac{216}\pi-\frac{108}\pi=\frac{108}\pi$.

**Answer: $\frac{108}\pi$**

arml-1997-individual-03.title: Look at the end of each losing streak
arml-1997-individual-03.body:
The winning percentage is lowest at the end of a losing streak. After $n$ blocks of wins and the following losing streaks, the team has $3n$ wins and $1+2+\dots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2$ losses. The wins are exactly $25\%$ of the games when $4\cdot3n=3n+\frac{n(n+1)}2$, i.e. $18=n+1$, $n=17$. So after $51$ wins and $153$ losses ($204$ games) the percentage is exactly $25\%$.

During the next block, the team wins $3$ more (so $54$ wins, $207$ games) and then loses $x$ games: we need $\frac{54}{207+x}<\frac14$, i.e. $207+x>216$, $x>9$, so $x=10$. Then $N=207+10=217$.

**Answer: 217**

arml-1997-individual-04.title: Work backwards from a fixed point
arml-1997-individual-04.body:
$x_i=x_3$ for all $i>3$ means $x_3$ is a fixed point: $4x-x^2=x$, so $x_3=0$ or $3$.

- If $x_3=0$: $f(x_2)=0$ gives $x_2=0$ or $4$; $x_2\ne x_3$ forces $x_2=4$. Then $f(x_1)=4$: $(x_1-2)^2=0$, $x_1=2$. The sequence $2,4,0,0,\dots$ has $x_1,x_2,x_3$ distinct.
- If $x_3=3$: $f(x_2)=3$ gives $x_2=1$ or $3$; so $x_2=1$. Then $f(x_1)=1$: $x_1^2-4x_1+1=0$, $x_1=2\pm\sqrt3$. The sequences $2\pm\sqrt3,1,3,3,\dots$ work.

So $x_1\in\{2,\ 2+\sqrt3,\ 2-\sqrt3\}$: $3$ values.

**Answer: 3**

arml-1997-individual-05.title: Linear constraint
arml-1997-individual-05.body:
Let the first term be $x>0$ and the common difference $y>0$ (increasing). The sum is $\frac{1999}2(2x+1998y)=1$, so $x+999y=\frac1{1999}$. Since $x>0$, $y<\frac1{999\cdot1999}$, and $y>0$ with $x\to0$ attaining values arbitrarily close to $\frac1{999\cdot1999}$. So the possible values of $y$ fill the interval $\left(0,\frac1{999\cdot1999}\right)$, of width $\frac1{999\cdot1999}=\frac1{(1000-1)(2000-1)}=\frac1{1997001}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{1997001}$**

arml-1997-individual-06.title: Conjugates and a recurrence
arml-1997-individual-06.body:
$\tan\frac\pi{12}=\tan\left(\frac\pi3-\frac\pi4\right)=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{1+\sqrt3}=2-\sqrt3$ and $\cot\frac\pi{12}=2+\sqrt3$. So the number is $N=a_{1997}$ where $a_n=(2-\sqrt3)^n+(2+\sqrt3)^n$. The two numbers are roots of $t^2=4t-1$, so $a_n=4a_{n-1}-a_{n-2}$ with $a_0=2$, $a_1=4$: these are integers. Modulo $9$: $a_0,a_1,\dots=2,4,5,7,5,4,2,4,\dots$ — it repeats with period $6$ ($a_6\equiv2$, $a_7\equiv4$). Since $1997=6\cdot332+5$, $a_{1997}\equiv a_5\equiv4\pmod 9$.

**Answer: 4**

arml-1997-individual-06.title: Binomial theorem
arml-1997-individual-06.body:
Expanding $(2+\sqrt3)^{1997}+(2-\sqrt3)^{1997}$, the terms with $\sqrt3$ cancel and the terms with $\binom{1997}{2k}$ for $k\ge2$ are multiples of $3^2=9$. So $N\equiv2\left(2^{1997}+\binom{1997}2\,2^{1995}\cdot3\right)\pmod9$, which equals $2^{1998}+1997\cdot998\cdot3\cdot2^{1996}$. With $2^6\equiv1$: $2^{1998}\equiv1$, $2^{1996}=2^{6\cdot332+4}\equiv2^4\equiv7$, $1997\equiv8$, $998\equiv8$ (mod $9$). So $N\equiv1+8\cdot8\cdot7\cdot3\equiv1+3\cdot(64\cdot7)\equiv1+3\cdot(1\cdot7)=22\equiv4\pmod9$.

**Answer: 4**

arml-1997-individual-07.title: Classify chords by direction
arml-1997-individual-07.body:
Number the vertices $0,\dots,9$ around the polygon. Chords $\{i,j\}$ with the same value of $i+j\pmod{10}$ are parallel, and these are all the parallel classes. There are $10$ classes.

- $i+j$ odd ($5$ classes): each class has $5$ chords: two sides, two diagonals joining vertices two apart, and one diameter. So $3$ diagonals: $\binom32=3$ pairs.
- $i+j$ even ($5$ classes): the two vertices on the symmetry axis are unpaired, leaving $4$ chords, all diagonals: $\binom42=6$ pairs.

Total: $5\cdot3+5\cdot6=45$.

**Answer: 45**

arml-1997-individual-08.title: Rationalise with t = cube root of 2
arml-1997-individual-08.body:
Let $t=\sqrt[3]2$. Then $(t+1)^3=t^3+3t^2+3t+1=3(t^2+t+1)$ (using $t^3=2$). Multiply by $t-1$: $(t+1)^3(t-1)=3(t^3-1)=3$, so $t-1=\frac3{(t+1)^3}$ and
$$\sqrt[3]{t-1}=\frac{\sqrt[3]3}{t+1}=\frac{\sqrt[3]3\,(t^2-t+1)}{t^3+1}=\frac{\sqrt[3]3\,(t^2-t+1)}3=\frac{t^2-t+1}{\sqrt[3]9}.$$
With $t=\sqrt[3]2$ this is $\frac{\sqrt[3]4-\sqrt[3]2+1}{\sqrt[3]9}=\sqrt[3]{\tfrac49}-\sqrt[3]{\tfrac29}+\sqrt[3]{\tfrac19}$. So $a+b+c=\frac49-\frac29+\frac19=\frac13$.

**Answer: $\frac13$**

arml-1997-individual-tb.title: The top block of constant floor
arml-1997-individual-tb.body:
For $1936=44^2\le n\le1997<45^2$ we have $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor=44$. So for $1936\le k<1997$, $S_{1997}-S_k=44(1997-k)=4\cdot11\cdot(1997-k)$. This is a perfect square iff $11(1997-k)$ is a square, i.e. $1997-k$ is $11$ times a square. The smallest value of $1997-k$ (largest $k$) is $11$, giving $k=1986$.

**Answer: 1986**
